supplement.where: Appendices A-H are included on PDF pp. 26-64. A separate supplementary dataset is mentioned on p. 10 (section 3.7), and external XLSX tables are named in Appendix G (pp. 56-58); no download URL is stated. The false flag refers to those external materials, not to the included appendices.
supplement.holds: The included appendices provide rubrics, fixed-effect coefficients/SEs, marginal means/CIs and mediation results, including creative-performance Tables 28-29 (pp. 52-53) and BDI-adjusted Tables 31-32 (pp. 54-55). The missing supplementary dataset holds coded exemplars. External SI_z_gain_EMMs_BDI_minus.xlsx, SI_z_gain_EMMs_BDI_plus.xlsx and SI_z_gain_CR2_BDI_CR2.xlsx contain complete performance-gain moderation EMMs/simple contrasts (p. 58, section G.6); analogous SI_TS, SI_PS and SI_GDQ files contain other outcomes' moderation results (pp. 56-57).

paper_design_summary: In the main online experiment, 905 analyzed Prolific participants completed an individual task, discussed it in a human-only or hybrid triad with undisclosed supportive/contrarian AI teammates, then completed the task individually again; triads were randomly assigned to conditions (pp. 2-6). The creative task required a movie plot, scored by blinded trained researchers for originality, elaboration and coherence; the paper analyzed standardized individual gains and also scored discussion transcripts, alongside self-reported team climate and AI detectability (pp. 7-13, 28, 33). A separate 15-person pilot assessed perceived humanness of AI teammates and supplied no creativity outcome (p. 8).

studies.label: Main experiment: three tasks crossed with six team/persona conditions

assignment.what_was_assigned: Participants were randomly formed into triads, and triads were randomly assigned to human-only versus hybrid compositions with supportive, contrarian or mixed AI personas. Each participant completed one task domain; the factorial design crossed task with condition. AI involvement was undisclosed. Allocation mechanisms and allocation-stage counts are not specified (p. 2; pp. 4-6, section 3.2 and Figure 2).
assignment.quote: Triads were randomly assigned to human-only teams or to groups that included one or two AI agents programmed with distinct personas, supportive or contrarian.
assignment.locator: p. 2, Introduction; pp. 4-6, section 3.2 and Figure 2
assignment.prereg_locator: No preregistration statement or identifier found in the full PDF, including appendices.

participants.exclusions: The paper says 1,047 initially entered, not that 1,047 were randomized. Excluded: attention-check failure n = 36; inadequate discussion engagement n = 67 (fewer than five messages and average message length below 20 characters); incomplete post-task survey n = 20; mismatch between individual and discussion task n = 19 (pp. 3-4, section 3.1). Primary analyses retain 905 people in 572 groups. A further 34 people with display-name mismatches are omitted only from BDI-related analyses, leaving 871 people; they remain in other analyses (p. 4). Table 2 is recorded as analyzed task-by-condition counts, not pre-exclusion randomization counts. No intention-to-treat analysis is claimed.
participants.who: English-fluent adults recruited through Prolific between 21 August 2025 and 20 September 2025; eligibility states ages 18-65 (p. 3, section 3.1). The 905-person count spans all three task domains; it is not the creative-task-only sample. Creative cell counts are separately retained in arms (p. 6, Table 2).
participants.country: Individual countries not stated. The reported regions are North America/Central America, South America, Europe, Africa, Asia and Australia (p. 4, Table 1).
participants.quote: After applying these exclusions, the final analytic sample for the primary analyses comprised 𝑁= 905 participants, clustered within 572 three-person groups.
participants.locator: pp. 3-4, section 3.1 and Table 1; p. 6, Table 2; p. 52, Table 28

ai_tool.how_used: Generative conversational agents acted as undisclosed teammates in synchronous group chat, using supportive or contrarian system prompts (pp. 5, 7-8, sections 3.2 and 3.4-3.5; pp. 29-31, Appendix B). They contributed and responded to the developing discussion under probabilistic scheduling and turn-taking constraints. This is social participation by an AI teammate, not a comparison of standalone AI and human stories. The document does not identify the underlying model, provider, version or sampling settings.

task.description: The eligible task was movie-plot brainstorming: develop characters, setting, key events and resolution, with AGI central to a plot beginning 'In the year 2045, the world's first AGI unexpectedly...' (p. 28, Appendix A.3; p. 7, section 3.3). Participants produced baseline and post-discussion individual responses around a group ideation phase (pp. 5-6). Other randomized task domains were survival-item ranking and an autonomous-vehicle moral dilemma (pp. 6-7, 26-28). They are part of the same experiment but are not scored as creative-writing outcomes here.
task.duration: Group discussion lasted 10 minutes (p. 5, section 3.2; p. 6, Figure 2). Individual pre/post writing durations and total session duration are not stated.

outcomes.name: Creative-writing individual performance gain (composite)
outcomes.question: after_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Creative-task component of the paper's standardized individual performance gain. Two independent researchers trained in education and psychology, blinded to condition, scored pre- and post-discussion stories; final ratings were averaged across raters (pp. 9-10, section 3.7). The story rubric comprises originality, elaboration, and coherence, each scored 1-5 (p. 33, Table 9); Table 6 reports a total score (p. 11). Gain is post-task minus baseline and continuous outcomes were standardized before analysis (p. 11, section 3.9). The precise total-score aggregation and standardization reference population are not fully specified. The primary LMM pools all tasks, includes Task x Condition and a group random intercept, and reports group-clustered CR2 inference with Satterthwaite degrees of freedom and Holm adjustment (pp. 12-13, section 3.11; p. 52, Table 28). Creative is the reference task, so condition main effects in Table 28 are creative-task contrasts, not effects averaged over tasks. Table 29 gives estimated marginal means and their own SEs/CIs, not raw arm means/SDs (p. 53). Conventional LMM inference, BDI-adjusted models/EMMs (pp. 54-55, Tables 31-32), and BDI moderation (pp. 56-58, Table 34 and section G.6) are variants of this outcome. Full moderation EMMs and simple contrasts are relegated to external XLSX files. Phase C repeats the task individually after AI-containing discussion, so this is immediate after_ai, not a delayed transfer test (pp. 5-6).
outcomes.delay: Same session, after the group discussion (pp. 5-6, section 3.2 and Figure 2); no later-session follow-up.

outcomes.name: Creative-story originality (post-discussion; baseline also rated)
outcomes.question: after_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: One of the creative-writing rubric dimensions, rated 1-5 for novelty, surprising combinations and freedom from predictable genre conventions (p. 33, Table 9). Two trained education/psychology researchers independently rated submissions, blinded to condition (pp. 9-10, section 3.7). Measured at baseline and post-discussion; Table 6 reports inter-rater reliability only for the separate dimension (p. 11). No arm-level originality means, SDs or treatment contrasts are printed. The dimension contributes to S1-O1; an absent subscale effect is not coded as a null finding. The scored post-discussion story is individually produced in Phase C (pp. 5-6).
outcomes.delay: Same session, after the group discussion (pp. 5-6, section 3.2 and Figure 2); no later-session follow-up.

outcomes.name: Creative-story elaboration (post-discussion; baseline also rated)
outcomes.question: after_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: One of the creative-writing rubric dimensions, rated 1-5 for detail about characters, setting, events and the story world (p. 33, Table 9). Two trained education/psychology researchers independently rated submissions, blinded to condition (pp. 9-10, section 3.7). Baseline and post-discussion reliability is reported in Table 6 (p. 11), but separate condition means, SDs and treatment contrasts are absent. This is rated detail, not a reported word-count outcome. It contributes to S1-O1. The post-discussion story is individually produced in Phase C (pp. 5-6).
outcomes.delay: Same session, after the group discussion (pp. 5-6, section 3.2 and Figure 2); no later-session follow-up.

outcomes.name: Creative-story coherence (post-discussion; baseline also rated)
outcomes.question: after_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: One of the creative-writing rubric dimensions, rated 1-5 for logical consistency, connected story elements and cohesive narrative construction (p. 33, Table 9). Coded as usefulness because it assesses the quality of the story, rather than novelty. Two trained education/psychology researchers independently rated submissions, blinded to condition (pp. 9-10, section 3.7). Table 6 reports baseline/post-discussion inter-rater reliability (p. 11); separate condition means, SDs and effects are not printed. It contributes to S1-O1. The post-discussion story is individually produced in Phase C (pp. 5-6).
outcomes.delay: Same session, after the group discussion (pp. 5-6, section 3.2 and Figure 2); no later-session follow-up.

outcomes.name: Group discussion quality during creative ideation (composite)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Expert-coded quality of the creative-task chat transcript, comprising idea generation and sharing, collaborative engagement, and progression and synthesis; each dimension is rated 1-5 (p. 33, Table 8). The two blinded education/psychology researchers rated the transcripts, with ratings averaged across raters (pp. 9-10, section 3.7); dimension ratings were averaged to a group composite (pp. 11-12, section 3.9). This evaluates observable ideation and collaboration processes, not the originality of a final story, and is retained separately from the core creativity score. The full Task x Condition OLS has one observation per group; n_units refers to the pooled model across all tasks, not solely Creative (pp. 12-13; p. 47, Table 24). Listed contrasts are for Creative, the reference task. CR2 inference and Holm adjustment are used for directions. Estimated marginal means in Table 25 have separately reported SEs and CIs (p. 48). BDI-adjusted models (pp. 49-50, Tables 26-27), exploratory BDI simple contrasts (p. 57, Table 37), and linguistic mediation (pp. 59-64, Appendix H) are variants of the same discussion-quality measure. AI agents are active in Phase B while the transcript is produced (pp. 5-6).
outcomes.delay: During the group discussion (pp. 5-6, section 3.2 and Figure 2).

outcomes.name: Creative discussion: idea generation and sharing
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Expert-rated transcript dimension, scored 1-5 from sparse or unsupported contributions to rich, detailed contributions from group members (p. 33, Table 8; pp. 9-10, section 3.7). Retained as an ideation-process measure, not a numerical fluency count and not an across-people diversity metric. Separate-dimension inter-rater reliability is reported in Table 6 (p. 11), but no arm-level effects or means are printed. It contributes to S1-O5. Creative-specific numbers of groups are not stated.
outcomes.delay: During the group discussion (pp. 5-6, section 3.2 and Figure 2).

outcomes.name: Creative discussion: collaborative engagement
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Expert-rated transcript dimension, scored 1-5 for acknowledgement, building on or challenging others' ideas, and integration producing new insights (p. 33, Table 8; pp. 9-10, section 3.7). This is a scored interaction-process component, not a self-report or story-creativity score. Table 6 reports dimension reliability (p. 11); no separate arm-level effects or means are printed. It contributes to S1-O5. Creative-specific numbers of groups are not stated.
outcomes.delay: During the group discussion (pp. 5-6, section 3.2 and Figure 2).

outcomes.name: Creative discussion: progression and synthesis
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Expert-rated transcript dimension, scored 1-5 for moving the discussion toward a conclusion, integrating ideas and reaching shared understanding (p. 33, Table 8; pp. 9-10, section 3.7). This is an interaction-process component, not a correct-answer convergent-thinking test. Table 6 reports dimension reliability (p. 11); separate arm-level effects or means are not printed. It contributes to S1-O5. Creative-specific numbers of groups are not stated.
outcomes.delay: During the group discussion (pp. 5-6, section 3.2 and Figure 2).

studies.label: Independent pilot: perceived humanness of AI teammate scheduling

assignment.what_was_assigned: All pilot participants interacted with two AI teammates using the selected scheduling protocol. No no-AI comparison, alternative protocol comparison or randomized allocation is reported (p. 8, section 3.5).
assignment.quote: The selected scheduling configuration was subsequently evaluated in an independent pilot study to assess perceived humanness.
assignment.locator: p. 8, section 3.5 (structure refers only to repeated ratings of two teammates, not randomized treatment order)

arms.name: Pilot: selected scheduling protocol
arms.description: Each human interacted with two AI teammates and rated their perceived humanness (p. 8, section 3.5). Persona composition not stated.

participants.exclusions: No pilot exclusions stated. Pilot participants and data were not included in the primary experiment (p. 8, section 3.5).
participants.who: Fifteen pilot participants; recruitment source and demographic characteristics are not separately stated (p. 8, section 3.5).
participants.quote: Fifteen participants each interacted with two AI teammates under this protocol, yielding a total of 30 humanness ratings on a 7-point Likert scale (1 = strongly disagree, 7 = strongly agree).

ai_tool.how_used: Two conversational AI teammates per participant under the scheduling protocol subsequently used in the main experiment; the pilot assessed human-like participation (p. 8, section 3.5).

task.description: Interaction with AI teammates followed by perceived-humanness ratings. The pilot's task content is not specified; no creativity/diversity score on participant output is reported (p. 8, section 3.5).

sample_overlap.shares_participants_with: No reuse of another paper's participants is stated; the main paper describes new Prolific recruitment. The independent pilot explicitly does not overlap the main analysis sample.
sample_overlap.quote: This pilot study was conducted separately from the main experiment, and neither the participants nor the data were included in the primary analyses.

company_involvement.description: No company funding, author affiliation or company role is reported. Author affiliations on the title page are universities; the AI vendor is not identified.
company_involvement.locator: p. 1, author affiliations; pp. 7-8 and 29-31, AI implementation descriptions

eligibility.reason: S1 randomly assigns triads to human-only or AI-containing configurations (p. 2; pp. 4-6, section 3.2/Figure 2). It analyzes 905 people across tasks (p. 4, section 3.1), and the Creative arm counts alone exceed the threshold: Table 2 directly reports 90 people in Creative H3, 62 in H2_C, 57 in H2_S, 30 in H1_C, 29 in H1_S and 30 in H1_M (p. 6). Blinded trained raters score actual movie-plot responses, including originality, elaboration and coherence (pp. 9-11; p. 33, Table 9), and creative-specific performance contrasts appear in Table 28 (p. 52). These are immediate after_ai outcomes because the scored post-task response is completed individually after the AI-containing discussion (pp. 5-6). Human partners make H3 an active comparator, so relevant AI-versus-H3 contrasts are ai_vs_active. This is an assistance experiment, not ai_vs_human. The separate pilot is below the people threshold and measures perceived humanness only.

one_line_finding: Following the discussion, creative-writing gains showed no clear advantage from AI teammates: H2_S versus H3 beta = 0.336, CR2 SE = 0.184, p = .074, Holm p = 1.00; the other creative AI-versus-H3 contrasts also had Holm p = 1.00 (p. 52, Table 28).
open_questions: Which generative model/version was used? The persona and scheduling sections and full prompts do not name it (pp. 7-8, 29-31).
Can the external XLSX moderation outputs and supplementary coded-exemplar dataset be obtained? They are named but have no download URL in the PDF (p. 10; pp. 56-58).

How exactly were the creative rubric dimensions aggregated, and over which population were performance gains standardized? The document gives dimensions, pre/post scoring and standardization but no fully explicit formula (pp. 9-13, 33, 51-55).
Are separate treatment statistics available for originality, elaboration and coherence, and for the discussion components? Only component reliability and rubric anchors are printed (pp. 11, 33).

Why do Appendices E and G call BDI baseline depression/depressive symptoms (pp. 38, 56), whereas the methods define it as the Balanced Detection Index (pp. 10-11)? Treat BDI-adjusted/moderation results cautiously until clarified.

The exploratory discussion-quality contrasts in Table 37 repeat the same printed estimate for every task and BDI level (p. 57). Verify them against the referenced XLSX rather than treating the repeated entries as independent precise effects.

Discussion transcript measures are retained as other process outcomes for completeness; their inclusion in a creativity synthesis needs adjudication. Eligibility here is supported by the scored story outcome regardless (pp. 11-12, 33).
notes: Read the complete markdown conversion and checked relevant methods, counts, rubric anchors and statistics against the PDF. Page locators refer to physical PDF pages; there are 64 pages, although the footers say 'of 65'. The title-page arXiv version/date is used, not an inferred later version. S1 is one factorial experiment, not three independent studies; S2 is the explicitly independent humanness pilot. The expert design panel described in section 3.5 is an implementation-development step, not another creativity study. Arms are listed as task-by-condition cells to preserve printed people counts without deriving unprinted totals. The H3 comparator consists of human collaborators, and all AI-versus-H3 contrasts share that comparator within a task. No effect sizes, contrast CIs, missing SDs or missing subgroup totals were calculated. For the primary individual outcome, estimates are printed coefficients on a standardized gain outcome, not an independently reconstructed Cohen's d. Primary versus BDI-adjusted analyses and subgroup/moderation analyses are not separate studies. Component outcomes without treatment statistics are retained with empty contrasts rather than claiming no effect. Complete outcome inventory from tables/figures/appendices: individual performance gain (creative-story total and originality, elaboration, coherence; ethical-reasoning total and problem recognition, argumentation, perspective-taking; survival-ranking error improvement); group discussion total and idea generation/sharing, engagement, progression/synthesis; self-reported psychological safety and teamwork satisfaction; AI sensitivity, human specificity, unsure-response rate, AI over-ascription and the BDI; linguistic clout, tone, positive/negative emotion, prosocial language, politeness, conflict, moralising, communication, plus assent and utterance length/word count mentioned in section 4.6; pilot perceived humanness (pp. 8-14, 15-20, 33-37, 39-64). The noncreative analytical and ethical performance measures, self-reports, detection checks and AI-language/persona measures are inventoried here but are not coded as creativity effects. No across-people output diversity measure is reported; within-discussion idea variety is not coded as diversity. Pilot humanness: 15 people supplied 30 ratings on a 7-point scale, M = 5.43, SD = 1.07 (p. 8, section 3.5); these are perceptions of AI, not participant creative-output scores. No outcomes were omitted because of the form's outcome limit.
